Harry observes that Malfoy had lowered his wand before the Death Eaters arrived. After the killing, Snape seizes Malfoy by the scruff of the neck and forces him through the door. The book explicitly states that Harry 'did not believe that Malfoy would have killed Dumbledore' and notes 'the tiniest drop of pity mingled with his dislike.' Draco's expression at Dumbledore's death is not described in detail in the corpus.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Draco 'stunned, staring at the empty place where Dumbledore stood only seconds before' after Snape kills him. The visual of Draco's frozen shock is present. What is lost is the book's explicit note of Malfoy's wand having dropped — the clearest signal of his choice — which Harry specifically observes and which underpins Harry's later reflection.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book makes Harry's observation of Malfoy's dropping wand explicit and uses it as the basis for Harry's post-tower reflection ('He did not believe that Malfoy would have killed Dumbledore'). The film renders Draco's choice ambiguous through stunned inaction rather than an observable physical lowering of the wand. This slightly reduces the clarity of Draco's moral choice at the climax, though the film does convey his inability to act through his trembling and hesitation throughout the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Unbreakable Vow scene, Narcissa and Snape
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's Unbreakable Vow scene contains Narcissa's extended, desperate pleading — she falls at Snape's feet, clutches his robes, weeps — and Bellatrix's specific challenge that Snape is a coward who will 'slither back into his hole.' Crucially, the book has Bellatrix articulate her contempt for Snape in detail and her astonishment when he agrees. The scene also establishes, through Narcissa's dialogue, that Draco 'isn't shrinking away from his duty, he seems glad of a chance to prove himself, excited at the prospect' (from Bellatrix), which is important context for Draco's initial attitude.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses the scene significantly. Narcissa's emotional breakdown is present but abbreviated. Bellatrix's challenge ('It's just empty words... he'll slither back into his hole. Bloody coward') is present. However, the specific detail that Draco himself 'seems glad of a chance to prove himself, excited at the prospect' — the line that establishes his initial willing eagerness — is absent from the film's version. The film skips directly to Snape's offer to help and the Vow itself.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Bellatrix's observation that Draco is initially 'excited' and 'glad' to prove himself is an important early characterisation note that contextualises his later deterioration — he started willing and proud, and was broken by the reality of the task. The film's omission of this detail means the audience begins Draco's arc without understanding his initial emotional state, slightly flattening the arc from eagerness to terror.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH1 - Drawing Room / Malfoy Manor opening (Scene 3)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Draco staring up at Charity Burbage's body in terror, glancing quickly at Voldemort and away again, terrified to make eye contact. When Voldemort asks 'What say you, Draco?' about babysitting the werewolf cubs, Draco looks in terror at his father, then catches his mother's eye and she shakes her head almost imperceptibly. Draco is shown as a terrified teenager trapped in a situation he cannot control, with internal family communication conveying shared dread. When Charity is killed, Draco falls out of his chair onto the floor - a visceral, involuntary physical reaction.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film script notes only that 'Draco nervously stares at the body above' and later 'Draco watches a teardrop strike the table.' The specific moment of Voldemort singling Draco out with the humiliating 'babysit the cubs' question is entirely absent. The subtle family dynamic - Narcissa's barely perceptible head shake, Draco's terrified glance at his father, the silent communication under Voldemort's nose - is lost. Draco falling from his chair when Charity is killed is not scripted.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's drawing room scene is the primary establishment of Draco's psychological state at the saga's opening: he is not a triumphant Death Eater but a frightened boy whose family is being publicly humiliated and punished. The specific singling-out by Voldemort, the silent family communication, and the physical collapse at the murder all characterize him as a victim of circumstance rather than a willing participant. Losing these beats softens the portrait of his captivity and reduces the audience's basis for later sympathy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH1 - Malfoy Manor arrival / identification scene (Scenes 5-8)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that it is Narcissa who first scrutinizes Harry's swollen face and takes charge of the identification process, calling Draco over herself. Draco approaches reluctantly, keeping his distance from Greyback, 'seemed as scared of looking at Harry as Harry was of looking at him.' When pressed by his father Lucius - who is 'beside himself with excitement' - Draco's expression is 'full of reluctance, even fear.' Draco says 'I can't - I can't be sure' and walks away toward the fireplace where his mother stood. When asked about Hermione he says 'I... maybe... yeah' and about Ron 'Yeah... it could be' with his back turned to the prisoners. The book makes explicit that Draco is deliberately not identifying them. Harry notices Draco's face up close: while his father looked excited, 'Draco's expression was full of reluctance, even fear.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Bellatrix take charge and summon Draco ('Get Draco,' 'Ah, Draco. Come here, darling'). Bellatrix physically nudges Draco forward until he is inches from Harry. Lucius steps forward with his wine glass 'sloshing' - a detail that diminishes him. Harry explicitly confronts Draco: 'Why didn't you tell her? Bellatrix. You knew it was me. But you didn't say anything.' This direct dialogue makes Draco's non-identification an explicit, acknowledged act visible to Blaise and Goyle, rather than the book's subtler ambiguous reluctance witnessed only by Harry. The film also has Bellatrix - not Narcissa - as the authority figure orchestrating the identification, reassigning dramatic control away from the Malfoy family unit.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's identification scene is carefully constructed so that Draco's non-identification is ambiguous and deniable - he could be genuinely unsure. This ambiguity is central to his moral arc: he is not heroically refusing, he is simply failing to condemn, which is a more complex and honest portrait of moral cowardice edging toward conscience. Harry's film line 'You knew it was me. But you didn't say anything' collapses this ambiguity into an explicit acknowledgment, robbing the moment of its moral complexity and making Draco's protection of Harry too overt and deliberate. Additionally, transferring authority in the scene from Narcissa to Bellatrix weakens the Malfoy family dynamic established in the books.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH1 - Drawing room confrontation / Bellatrix calls the Dark Lord (Scene 9)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that after Harry and Ron burst into the drawing room, 'Lucius, Narcissa, Draco and Greyback wheeled about' and jets of light fly from Draco's, Narcissa's, and Greyback's wands. When Bellatrix orders 'Draco, pick them up!' he retrieves the fallen wands. When the chandelier falls, 'Draco doubled over, his hands covering his bloody face.' Harry then 'leapt over an armchair and wrested the three wands from Draco's grip.' The book also establishes that it is Lucius Malfoy who summons Voldemort - 'Lucius Malfoy called the Dark Lord' is implied by Bellatrix's command structure - but critically in the book Bellatrix calls 'The Dark Lord is coming, Harry Potter' suggesting the summons has been made. The Cruciatus torture vision of Draco being forced to torture Rowle ('Draco, give Rowle another taste of our displeasure... Do it, or feel my wrath yourself') is book-established context for Draco's coercion.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film script has Bellatrix order 'Call him, Draco' - meaning summon Voldemort via the Dark Mark. Draco hesitates. But then 'Lucius doesn't, pulling up his sleeve and touching his finger to the DARK MARK on his forearm.' This transfers the act of summoning Voldemort from an ambiguous or Bellatrix-led moment to Lucius explicitly, while Draco's hesitation is noted but then bypassed. The net effect is that Draco's hesitation is staged as a beat but immediately overridden, giving him a visible moment of reluctance without consequence or follow-through.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film creates a staged hesitation for Draco that is immediately nullified by Lucius acting instead. This is actually a more damaging structural choice than simply having Draco comply: it gives Draco a visible moral moment and then resolves it externally, suggesting he would have refused but was preempted. This distorts his characterization - in the books his reluctance is subtler and his complicity more passive. The film's version risks reading as Draco being covertly heroic, which misrepresents his arc of gradual, reluctant drift away from Voldemort rather than active resistance.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH2 - Room of Requirement confrontation (Scenes 18-19)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Draco with Crabbe and Goyle (not Blaise). Crabbe is the dominant threat who repeatedly defies Draco's orders: 'I don't take your orders no more, Draco. You an' your dad are finished.' Draco repeatedly tries to prevent Crabbe from killing Harry - 'The Dark Lord wants him alive,' 'STOP! The Dark Lord wants him alive,' 'Don't kill him! DON'T KILL HIM!' - because Draco understands Voldemort's orders and is trying to fulfill them, not out of mercy. Draco is wandless after Hermione's spell, cowering 'behind a three-legged wardrobe.' His authority has completely collapsed - his henchmen have turned on him. The scene shows Draco's total loss of power and social standing among Death Eater circles.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces Crabbe with Blaise (likely for casting reasons). More significantly, the film gives Draco the opening confrontation line 'Well, well, what brings you here, Potter?' - a composed, almost theatrical opening. The film also adds the exchange where Harry asks why Draco didn't identify him at Malfoy Manor, and Draco's conflicted, twitching response. Goyle (filling Crabbe's role) sets the fire. The film removes the extended sequence where Draco desperately orders Crabbe to stop - the complete collapse of his authority among his own followers. The film's Draco is more composed and more overtly conflicted/sympathetic than the book's Draco, who is attempting to execute Voldemort's orders and finding even that denied to him.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Room of Requirement scene is a culminating moment for Draco's arc of diminishment: he has lost all power, his own henchmen defy him openly, and he is reduced to cowering. The film softens this by giving him a composed opening, staging him as visibly conflicted about Harry (the Malfoy Manor callback), and eliding the full humiliation of Crabbe's open defiance. The replacement of Crabbe with Blaise also loses the specific dynamic of a lifelong servant openly declaring 'you an' your dad are finished' - one of the most damning statements about the Malfoy family's collapsed status. This reduces the dramatic payoff of his arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH2 - Courtyard / Draco crossing to Voldemort's side (Scene 27)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that during the battle's lull, Draco is seen on the upper landing 'pleading with another masked Death Eater' saying 'I'm Draco Malfoy, I'm Draco, I'm on your side!' Harry Stunned the Death Eater as they passed, saving Draco. Ron then punched Draco from under the Cloak, and Ron yelled 'And that's the second time we've saved your life tonight, you two-faced bastard!' Draco's position in the battle is ambiguous and desperate - he is not fighting for either side but trying to survive. The book makes no scene of Draco publicly crossing to Voldemort's side in front of the assembled crowd.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film constructs a public scene in the courtyard where Lucius summons Draco forth in front of both factions. Draco hesitates, Lucius says 'Draco, don't be stupid,' Narcissa says 'Come, Draco' with quiet authority, and Draco crosses the gulf between factions while 'avoiding the baleful glances directed his way.' Ron mutters 'He saved your life' as Draco passes. Narcissa then hands Draco Harry's wand. Draco 'stares at it bleakly.' Voldemort says 'Well done, Draco.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most structurally damaging scene in the film corpus. The book never has Draco publicly cross to Voldemort's side in a staged, witnessed moment of apparent betrayal. The book's Draco is in a chaotic middle ground - not fighting for Voldemort, not fighting for Harry, just surviving. The film invents a public act of apparent collaboration that the book does not contain, which significantly damages audience perception of his character at a critical moment. Ron's line 'He saved your life' as Draco crosses is meant to add irony, but the visual of Draco walking to Voldemort's side - receiving Harry's wand from his mother and being praised by Voldemort - creates a definitive image of betrayal that the books deliberately avoid. The book preserves Draco's ambiguity to the end; the film stages a false climax of his moral failure just before the final battle resolves.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH2 - Room of Requirement escape / Draco's farewell (Scene 21)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that after escaping the fire, 'Draco fell off the broom and lay facedown, gasping, coughing, and retching' and his first words were 'C-Crabbe... C-Crabbe...' grieving for his dead friend. Ron says 'He's dead' harshly. Draco and Goyle then 'remained slumped hopelessly on the corridor floor; neither of them had wands.' They subsequently vanish from Harry's sight. The book gives Draco a genuine grief reaction for Crabbe - his companion since childhood - which humanizes him at a key moment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film script shows 'Draco, staring fearfully at Harry. Blaise scrambles up and off. Draco lingers briefly, then finally rises and follows, but as he reaches the end of the corridor, he looks back. He begins to say something, then continues on.' Ron says 'You're bloody well welcome! Prat.' The grief for Crabbe/Goyle's death is absent. Instead Draco is given a lingering, almost tender farewell look at Harry - beginning to say something he cannot say.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film replaces Draco's genuine grief for his dead childhood friend (a humanizing beat that shows he has real emotional bonds, not just calculated alliances) with a sentimental almost-moment directed at Harry. This is a net loss: it trades authentic characterization (grief, loss, the human cost of war even for those on the wrong side) for a more conventionally redemptive gesture toward the protagonist. Draco's relationship with Crabbe and Goyle, however limited, was real; the film's substitution of a wistful look at Harry is tonally false to the character.
